traveler: Arthur of Lotharingia (Wolfram von Eschenbach's Artus, King of Bertane)
title: The Round Table of Bertane: Karidoel to Schamilot
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Bertane and the Court at Karidoel

stops.name: Karidoel, the Court of Bertane
stops.campa: Where the lake water pools beneath the walls at Nantua, in the mountain country above the Ain, stands Karidoel, the castle Werner Greub gives to Wolfram's King Arthur of Bertane, a land carved from the broken empire of Charlemagne's grandsons. Here Arthur holds his court and his Round Table, and here Queen Guinevere keeps her ladies about her. Bertane is a young kingdom, stitched together from the ruin of Louis the Pious's sons' wars, and Karidoel is its beating heart: a hall of falconers and minstrels, of oaths sworn and fellowship kept, waiting for the stranger knights this restless age is about to send it.
suggested_refs: The site of medieval Nantua, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Karidoel
The abbey church of Saint-Michel at Nantua, the surviving medieval fabric of the town
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III (trans. Jessie L. Weston, 1894)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found - Wolfram von Eschenbach as a Historian, 'Wolfram the Historian' (trans. R.J. Kelder)
willehalminstitute.blogspot.com, 'Bertane, the Land of King Arthur' (ch. 11 of Greub's book)

stops.name: Karidoel, the Blood Before the Gate
stops.campa: Before the gate a stranger knight, Ither of Kukumerlant, all in red, has spilled a golden cup over Guinevere's lap and ridden off unpunished, no man of Arthur's circle daring the field. A boy fresh from the forest of Soltane, ignorant of arms and their names, begs leave of the queen and rides after him bearing only a herdsman's javelin. He casts it through eye and neck; Ither falls dead on the grass before Nantes. Weeping over the body whose armor he cannot unbuckle, the boy is armed in the dead man's red mail by the squire Iwanet, and rides on: Ither's slayer and his heir both.
stops.quote: There the javelin swiftly sped, and thro' eye and neck it struck him, and the knight on the plain lay dead... So the armour was reft from the dead man, 'fore Nantes on the grassy plain, and they did it upon the living, o'er whose dealings did folly reign.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The grassy plain before Nantua where Ither's red armor passes to the boy who killed him
Manuscript illuminations of Ither the Red Knight in the Parzival codices (e.g. Cod. Pal. germ. 339)
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book III (trans. Weston)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, 'Wolfram the Historian'

stops.name: Karminal, the Hunting Lodge
stops.campa: North of Bertane, above the young river Birs, rises Karminal, the hunting lodge Greub sets in the deep wood Wolfram calls Brizljan: the castle later ages will call Dorneck. Arthur keeps late summer here, hawks flown from the walls, hounds coursing the oak slopes toward the plain of the Birs below. It is a place between the court's pomp and the wild wood's law, half hall and half forest camp, and it is from here that Arthur's fellowship rides down toward the river, into whatever adventure the season sends among the falcons and the geese.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Dorneck Castle above Dornach, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Karminal
The Brizljan forest of the poem, the wooded hills between Dorneck and the Birs valley
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, 'Wolfram the Historian'
Wikipedia, 'Dorneck Castle'

stops.name: The Oath Before the Search
stops.campa: For eight days Arthur's fellowship has ridden its own and stranger ground, hunting no game but a rumor: a Red Knight, unnamed, who has avenged them all on their old enemy Klamide without asking leave. Before the search goes further, Arthur calls in every man who can bear a shield and binds them by oath: whatever deeds of knighthood they may see, none shall venture a conflict without the king's own leave first given. Untrained hounds off the leash, he tells them, come to grief in strange country. It is the discipline of a court that means to make the unknown rider its own, and it will be sorely tested.
stops.quote: Now, 'tis well! Since we needs must go thro' many a stranger country, where many a stranger spear, and many a gallant hero are waiting us, I fear, if ye, like hounds untrainèd whose leash shall have slipped the hand of him who was late their master, shall roam free o'er all the land, much evil might there befall ye.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Arthur binding his knights before the search
suggested_refs: Arthur's oath-taking before the Round Table, as staged in medieval Parzival manuscripts
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Down to the Birs
stops.campa: The fellowship breaks camp at Karminal and descends through the Brizljan wood toward the river, tents and wagons and the queen's household following the falconers down the old paths. By evening the army pitches along the Birs on the stretch the poem calls Plimizoel, below Dornachbrugg where the valley opens. A thousand tents and more go up, on either side of the water as the poem counts them; and because the Table itself can never be carried out of Nantes, the court brings instead the great round silk that stands for it, folded on a wagon like a relic going to its next altar.
suggested_refs: The old bridge site at Dornachbrugg, on the Birs between Dornach and Arlesheim
sources: willehalminstitute.blogspot.com, 'Wolfram the Historian' (summary chronology)
Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)

segments.name: The Camp on the Birs, September 842

stops.name: The Camp on the Plimizoel Meadow
stops.campa: The army lies strung along the Birs below the bridge at Dornachbrugg, and into this camp ride, one after another, the players of the coming drama: Orilus and his wronged sister Jeschute, Klamide the conquered king, Cunneware of Lalant and her champion. Arthur receives each with the courtesy that is his whole art of rule, seats the great among the small, and remembers old griefs kindly. Guinevere sits at his side through it all, queen of a camp that is, for these few autumn days, the true seat of Bertane. The falconers ride out hawking by the water at dusk, and one of the hawks does not come back.
suggested_refs: The Birs riverbank below Dornachbrugg, the poem's Plimizoel in Greub's reading
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V-VI (trans. Weston)
willehalminstitute.blogspot.com, 'Wolfram the Historian'

stops.name: The Blood Drops in the Snow
stops.campa: Snow falls out of season on the woods above the camp, and Wolfram breaks in to say so: whatever men sing of Arthur happens at Whitsuntide or when May blossoms the meadow, never in snow. The lost falcon strikes a goose over a fallen tree; the bird escapes, and three drops of its blood fall crimson on the white ground. The young knight in red armor riding by, Parzival, reins in and cannot look away. White and red together are the face of his wife Kondwiramur, left at Pelrapeire. He sits his horse in a waking trance, lance upright, while the whole army watches and takes him for a challenger.
stops.quote: Say what hand hath painted these colours that here I see? Kondwiramur, I think well, these tints sure shall liken thee!... Red as blood-drops and white as the snowdrift, it rejoiceth me evermore!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The blood-drops-in-the-snow scene, one of the most illustrated episodes of the Parzival manuscript tradition
Stollenrain, Arlesheim, the site Greub's readers give to the three drops
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Segramors Unhorsed
stops.campa: Cunneware's squire, riding out toward Lalant, spies the trance-bound stranger and turns back to cry shame on the camp for letting one knight sit unchallenged so near. Segramors, Guinevere's kinsman, tears the sable coverlet off the sleeping king and queen at dawn to beg leave, and the queen herself wins Arthur's grudging consent. He gallops out, taunts the silent knight, and charges; Parzival, whose wheeling horse swings the blood-drops out of his sight just long enough, wakes to answer the blow and unseats him in a single pass. Segramors picks himself from the snow more embarrassed than hurt, and the stranger sinks back at once into his waking dream.
stops.quote: Now it seemeth but ill to me that thus near our army lieth, and our presence rejoiceth thee!... I call on thee here to yield thee, ere I put thee to shame, Sir Knight!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Segramors to the silent knight
suggested_refs: The joust of Segramors, illustrated beside the blood-drops scene in the Parzival codices
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Keye's Fall
stops.campa: Kay the seneschal, stung by Segramors's shame, wins the same reluctant leave and rides out mocking, offers the entranced knight a hempen halter as to a runaway thief, and smites his helmet with the spear-shaft to wake him. Kay's lance does pierce the shield; the payment is swifter. Parzival's counter-blow throws horse and rider onto the same fallen tree where the geese had hidden, and Kay's right arm and left leg break between stone and saddle-bow, his girths and saddle and bells of gold shattered over the snow. Wolfram will not let him be despised for it: one blow, he says, repaid two, and the other was Cunneware's.
stops.quote: Sir Knight, since thou thus our king hast shamed, thou shalt hear my counsel, for wisdom perchance 'twill bring; thou shalt hang thee a hempen halter around thy neck straightway... Low on the snow I'll lay thee!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Kay to the silent knight
suggested_refs: The joust of Kay (Keye), Arthur's seneschal, broken on the same fallen tree as the blood-drops
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)

stops.name: The Round Table Spread on the Plimizoel
stops.campa: Gawain ends the enchantment by the plainest means: he lays a cloth of silk and sendal over the blood-stained snow, and the spell goes out with the colors. Then Arthur has the second silk unrolled, the one woven in Acraton and carried from heathen lands, wide and shapen round, and spread on the flowering meadow where neither tree nor tent hinders it. The Table cannot be borne out of Nantes, so here they show its semblance. No high seat and no low; knight, lady and maiden alike are welcome at the ring. Arthur leads Parzival to it by the hand, and the fellowship is complete for one afternoon.
stops.quote: Then a silk in Acraton woven, they laid on the grassy sward, 'twas brought from far lands of paynim, and 'twas shapen both wide and round... No high seat had they of honour, but all men were equal there.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The Round Table as a round silk spread on open ground, Wolfram's own doctrine of equal honor
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Cundrie's Curse and the Call to Chastel Marveil
stops.campa: The honor lasts an afternoon. Cundrie the sorceress rides in on her mule, boar-tusked and bear-eared, speaking French to the Breton king, and before Arthur's whole circle denounces Parzival by name: he sat before the wounded Grail King Anfortas and asked no question of pity, and for that silence he is cursed. She shames Arthur too, telling him the fame of the Table suffered for the friendship it swore. Then she turns from them both to call any knight bold enough to ride to Chastel Marveil, where four queens and four hundred maidens lie captive, and rides on weeping.
stops.quote: Thou son of high Pendragon, thyself, and thy Breton host, by thy deed hast thou shamed... The fame of thy Table Round it suffered for the friendship ye with Parzival did swear... 'The Red Knight' ye here do call him, the name of one who lay dead before Nantes, yet I tell thee unlike in their life are they!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Depictions of Cundrie la Sorcière denouncing Parzival, a set-piece of the illuminated Parzival tradition
Chastel Marveil identified by Werner Greub with the Isteiner Klotz on the Rhine
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 'Schastel Marveil'

stops.name: Kingrimursel's Challenge, and the Camp Broken
stops.campa: Before the shamed camp can recover, Kingrimursel, Landgrave of Schampfanzun, rides in and calls Gawain out by name to answer a charge of treason forty days hence in his own city; Gawain accepts and arms for departure. Then Ekuba, the young heathen queen of Janfuse, speaks up in the circle. Cundrie has already named the brother, she says; she can vouch for him, for she is his mother's cousin. He is Feirefis Angevin, king of Zassamank and Assagog, and his face is black and white together. By nightfall the camp breaks in three directions: Gawain toward his trial, Parzival toward the Grail, Arthur home to Karidoel.
suggested_refs: Schampfanzun, identified with Champagnole, where Gawain's trial is set forty days hence
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI (trans. Weston)
willehalminstitute.blogspot.com, 'Wolfram the Historian'

stops.name: Bems by the Korka, City of Löver
stops.campa: The empire the boy-emperors carved apart at Verdun this year has left Bertane inside Lothair's middle kingdom, and Arthur's court, wintering now more often than not from Karidoel, keeps long seasons at Bems, the city Wolfram sets by the little river Korka in the land he calls Löver: Beaune, on the Burgundian plain. Years turn over here while Gawain wanders, his forty-day trial grown into a longer quest, and while Parzival, cursed and silent, seeks Munsalvaesche alone. Arthur waits, as a king must, holding the middle of the story while its edges range far from him.
suggested_refs: Medieval Beaune on the Burgundian plain, identified by Werner Greub as Wolfram's Bems
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIII (trans. Weston)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, 'Wolfram the Historian'

stops.name: The Messenger from Gawain Reaches Bems
stops.campa: A footman reaches Bems from the Rhine with a letter that bears no seal and needs none. Gawain has broken a bough from King Gramoflanz's tree, and Gramoflanz, who stood unarmed and would not fight one man alone, named the terms himself once the names were out: the sixteenth day, at Ioflanz on the plain, and Arthur may come up from Bems by the Korka in eight days. So Gawain asks his uncle for the whole court as witness, and for the one man whose word can end a blood-feud too old to remember its own cause. Arthur sends the herald back in two days with his promise.
stops.quote: At Château Merveil; and on thy side thine uncle can others bring, from the land that he rules, King Arthur, and Löver its name shall be, and the city is Bems by the Korka... There lieth he now with his vassals, and hither can make his way, in eight days, with great joy; so I bid thee to meet me... at Ioflanz upon the plain.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIII, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), King Gramoflanz naming the day to Gawain
suggested_refs: The herald's ride from Kembs to Beaune, retracing the Rhine-Saône road of the ninth century
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIII (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Arthur Breaks Camp at Beaune
stops.campa: At dawn the second day after the herald's word, Arthur's household rides out of Bems in full array: Guinevere and her ladies among the columns, the great round silk on its wagon, knights of a dozen lands who have wintered at his court. The road runs east from the Burgundian plain toward the young mountains and the great river, five days of ordinary marching set against the vast distances the poem elsewhere claims for such journeys, because Bems and Ioflanze, on the ground Greub actually walks, lie closer to one another than the singer's rounder eight days would have it.
suggested_refs: The road from Beaune toward the Rhine, the route Werner Greub reconstructs for Arthur's march
sources: Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 'Schastel Marveil'

stops.name: Past Logrois in the Sundgau
stops.campa: On the third day the column passes within sight of Logrois, the fortress the poem gives to the duchess Orgeluse, which Greub sets on this ground at Landser in the Sundgau. The poem follows Arthur nowhere along this road and gives the march no incident; only the castle stands here, and it stands as the quarrel's own source. Orgeluse's love was killed by Gramoflanz, and her grief hired every knight who ever rode for her, Gawain among them. Arthur rides past the walls of the wrong that he is going to the Rhine to unmake, and the poem does not say whether he looks up at them.
suggested_refs: Landser in the Sundgau, identified by Werner Greub with the poem's Logrois despite the discrepancy in terrain
sources: Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 'Terre de Salvaesche' and 'Schastel Marveil'

stops.name: The Rhine Plain at Kembs, the Sixth of May
stops.campa: On the sixth day Arthur's column comes down onto the flat water-meadows of the Rhine north of Basle, the plain Wolfram calls Ioflanze, and finds Gawain's camp and Gramoflanz's already pitched over against one another, hosts a mile and more in length with the ladies' bridles ringing among them. Trumpets sound the king's arrival; Gawain rides out bareheaded to meet him, and Guinevere is welcomed by Queen Arnive, Gawain's own grandmother, found alive after Klingsor's long enchantment. Two armies gathered for a duel of honor become, in a single afternoon, one great encampment waiting to see whether it ends in war or a wedding.
suggested_refs: Kembs on the Rhine, identified by Werner Greub with Wolfram's Joflanze/Ioflanz
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV (trans. Weston)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, ch. 'Schastel Marveil'

stops.name: The Hosts Assembled
stops.campa: For two days the plain at Joflanze fills further: Klingsor's freed queens ride in from Chastel Marveil, Orgeluse's knights make camp beside Arthur's, and heralds go between the tents arranging precedence and truce. Arthur sends his own messengers to Gramoflanz to plead the Table's honor for Gawain, and is refused; the king will keep the day he swore. So Arthur weighs the old wrong that started the feud and works the other way instead, as he worked it on the Birs six years before, to see whether a king's word can settle what private killing cannot. It is the same discipline, tested now on two armies.
suggested_refs: The Rhine plain north of Basle, gathering-ground of the reconciliation
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Gawain and Parzival, Unknowing, at Arms
stops.campa: On the morning the Gramoflanz duel should be fought, Gawain rides early to the ground and finds a stranger there in unmarked armor. They joust on the dewy grass, both go down with their horses, and they fight on with swords until the shields are hewn to splinters and the hours run out. It is Parzival, and he has the better of it: Gawain is near beaten when Arthur's returning pages cry his name across the field. The stranger throws his weapon from his hand and weeps that his luckless hand has fought so sinful a strife. Gawain, unhelmed, tells him plainly the victory is his.
stops.quote: Alas! that with gallant Gawain I have foughten so fierce a fight, 'tis myself whom I here have vanquished, and my joy shall have taken flight... For thy kinsman am I, and cousin, and men call me Parzival!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The unrecognized duel of kinsmen, a recurring motif Wolfram repeats across the Grail cycle
Mönchsberg, the ground Greub's readers give to the combat with the unknown knight
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Gramoflanz Reconciled, Arthur's Peace
stops.campa: Arthur takes the quarrel out of the field entirely. With Brandelidelein of Punturtois, Gramoflanz's own uncle, he divides the work: Brandelidelein will bring his nephew round, Arthur will bring the Duchess. He rises from the feast, walks out to Gawain's tent, carries the terms back, and by the day's end has turned a duel to the death into a wedding. Orgeluse gives Gramoflanz the kiss of forgiveness for her slain love, weeping as she gives it; Gramoflanz and Gawain kiss and end the strife; and Arthur gives Itonje, Gawain's sister, to the king to wife, generous as ever with gifts that cost him nothing and restore everything.
stops.quote: Then Arthur the wise and courteous, he brought the tale again, and King Gramoflanz, for his garland, henceforward must mourn in vain... Then Gramoflanz and Sir Gawain with a kiss put an end to strife; and Arthur gave maid Itonjé to King Gramoflanz to wife.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: Arthur as peacemaker at Joflanze, arranging the marriage that ends the Gramoflanz feud
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Feirefiss, the Brother Both Black and White
stops.campa: A magnificent unknown knight lands from ships on the Rhine and rides into camp in armor sewn with jewels, seeking adventure; Parzival meets him at arms before either learns the other's name, and the fight goes hard until Parzival's sword shatters on the stranger's helm. The heathen could kill him now and says so, then will not: he flings his own blade away into the wood so the contest stands even. Only then does he ask what face Parzival's brother bears. Parzival answers on Ekuba's word, black and white as written parchment, and the heathen says: then that brother am I. They unhelm and embrace as kin.
stops.quote: Quoth Feirefis, 'Now, thou hero, by thy courteous breeding fair, since in sooth thou shalt have a brother, say, what face doth that brother bear?'... Quoth the Waleis, 'As written parchment, both black and white is he, for so hath Ekuba told me.' 'Then that brother am I alway,' quoth the heathen... hatred and wrath were slain here in a brotherly embrace.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)
suggested_refs: The meeting of Parzival and Feirefiss, illustrated in the Parzival manuscript tradition as the reconciliation of Christian and heathen kin
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV (trans. Weston)

stops.name: Cundrie's Second Coming, the Grail Crown
stops.campa: On Whitsun Saturday, six years to the season since she cursed him on the Birs, Cundrie the sorceress rides again into Arthur's camp, but kneels now before Parzival instead: the throne of the Grail has passed to him, she says, and Anfortas may at last be released from his long wound if Parzival will come and ask the question he once failed to ask. Arthur's whole court hears the reversal of that old shame. Parzival, Feirefiss and Cundrie ride out from Joflanze together toward Munsalvaesche, and the king's part in the story, though not the story itself, draws toward its close.
suggested_refs: Cundrie's second visitation, reversing her curse, illustrated as a mirror scene to the first in the manuscript tradition
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV (trans. Weston)

segments.name: The Road to Dianazdrun and Schamilot

stops.name: Dianazdrun, the Court Comes Home
stops.campa: Whitsunday crowns Parzival at Munsalvaesche and the great camp on the Rhine empties, every company taking the road it knows. Arthur turns his household back into the heart of Bertane, a week of ordinary marching down the Saône valley on the old Roman roads, away from the frontier and its enchantments. The court that has spent this whole story as a camp, a lodge, a riverside pavilion, comes at last to a city: Dianazdrun, the place later ages will call Dijon, seat of the dukes who will one day rule this same Burgundian land the poem has been quietly describing all along under other, older names.
suggested_refs: The old road from the upper Rhine to Dijon, retracing the Saône valley
sources: Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, 'Wolfram the Historian'

stops.name: Schamilot, the Round Table's Last Seat
stops.campa: Arthur comes at last to Schamilot, the seat by Dianazdrun that Weston renders with the only Camelot this whole poem contains: a low rise of ground outside Dijon where, five centuries hence, Duke Philip the Bold will raise the Chartreuse de Champmol as the necropolis of Burgundy's own dukes, and set Claus Sluter's mourning figures to weep in stone around it. The poem does not know that future and does not need to; it only sets the Round Table down here, at journey's end, on the ground that will keep faith with it, in its own fashion, for as long as Burgundy remembers its dead.
stops.quote: King Arthur to Camelot journeyed with many a hero true.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894); Weston notes this as the poem's only mention of Camelot, identified by Werner Greub with Champmol, Dijon
suggested_refs: The Chartreuse de Champmol, Dijon, and Claus Sluter's Well of Moses, raised on the ground Greub identifies as Wolfram's Schamilot
The ducal necropolis of Burgundy now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon
sources: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI (trans. Weston)
Werner Greub, How the Grail Sites Were Found, 'Wolfram the Historian'
Wikipedia, 'Chartreuse de Champmol'
